paper_title: Turns Matter: Advancing Streaming Video RL via Turn-Level Credit

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining a single trajectory-level advantage across turns. Such shared credit can reinforce redundant replies after earlier successes and discourage useful follow-ups after earlier failures. We propose TurnWise, a turn-level GRPO framework that aligns learning with individual streaming decisions. TurnWise addresses the mismatch between trajectory-level feedback and turn-level interaction, promoting informative responses and reducing redundancy. Specifically, turn-level credit assignment uses silence-completed prefix scoring to construct group-relative advantages from each decision's remaining return, separating its learning signal from earlier rewards. Turn-mean policy optimization averages token losses within each turn and then across turns, giving response and waiting decisions equal weight regardless of output length. These complementary designs improve streaming policy learning without a learned critic or additional rollouts. Extensive experiments show our method outperforms prior RL approaches for streaming video understanding.

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Streaming video understanding requires models to repeatedly decide whether to respond or continue observing. Recently, Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) has been applied to this setting, with existing approaches emphasizing reward design while retaining single trajectory-level advantage across turns. sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Streaming video understanding requires models to interpret an evolving visual world and interact while observations are still arriving [4, 19, 32]. Unlike offline video understanding [34], where the complete video is available before answering, streaming interaction unfolds through repeated decisions under partial observations. At each turn, model must decide whether to respond or continue observing [24, 26]. useful assistant should respond when new evidence warrants an answer, provide follow-up information when needed, and remain silent when another reply would add little value. The appropriate action therefore depends not only 1 Fig. 1 Shared advantages can reinforce redundant replies. GRPO assigns one trajectory-level advantage to all turns, so later repetitions may inherit positive credit from earlier successes. TurnWise subtracts group-relative accrued reward before each decision, allowing later turns to receive credit according to their remaining return. The dialogue is illustrative. The advantage plot uses recorded TurnWise advantages and the corresponding GRPO counterfactual. on the current visual evidence [7, 11, 30], but also on what the model has already communicated. Learning this sequence of response and waiting decisions requires feedback that reflects answer quality and interaction timing. Reinforcement learning [8, 2022] provides natural way to learn these decisions from interaction-level feedback, with recent approaches adopting Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) [21]. MMDuet2 [26] optimizes proactive interaction with PAUC-based rewards [25], while ThinkStream [16] combines incremental reasoning with rewards for correctness, format, and response timing. StreamPro [13] further incorporates both turn-level and trajectory-level rewards to assess individual responses and overall interaction quality. Reward design and short-span training [26] improve interaction feedback, but the trajectory-level GRPO formulations considered here still broadcast one advantage across decision turns. Turn-level scoring and turn-specific policy credit are therefore distinct design choices. good trajectory can contain bad turns, and bad trajectory can contain good turns. After successful early response, redundant reply may still inherit positive trajectory advantage, even if the reward penalizes repetition  (Fig. 1)  . Conversely, useful follow-up after earlier failures may receive negative advantage because the trajectory remains below the group average. In both cases, rewards accrued before the current decision influence its learning signal, potentially obscuring the value of responding or waiting at that turn. We therefore argue that streaming decisions learning signal should emphasize the return from that turn onward, rather than rewards accumulated earlier. Guided by this principle, we propose TurnWise, turn-level GRPO framework that aligns advantage estimation and loss aggregation with streaming decisions. Building on the return-to-go principle [22], TurnWise exploits the explicit waiting action to score each trajectory prefix with all remaining turns set to silence. Subtracting this prefix reference from the full trajectory reward yields remaining return, from which we construct group-relative, turn-specific advantages. Silence-completed prefix scoring converts trajectory feedback into turn-specific remaining-return advantages. The computation reuses existing rollout evaluations, requiring neither learned critic nor additional rollouts. 2 TurnWise couples turn-specific credit with equal weighting of response and waiting decisions. Under tokenmean aggregation, longer responses still receive larger aggregation weights than short waiting actions. We therefore introduce turn-mean loss aggregation, averaging token losses within each turn before averaging across turns within each trajectory. Turn-mean aggregation balances sampled response and waiting decisions directly in the RL objective, making each turns weight independent of its output length. Together, the two designs make the decision turn common unit for advantage estimation and loss aggregation, addressing both how turn receives credit and how its feedback is weighted during policy optimization. In summary, our contributions are as follows: We identify granularity mismatch in streaming video RL. Shared trajectory advantages can obscure the value of later decisions, while token-mean loss aggregation makes turn weights depend on response length. We introduce TurnWise, combining silence-completed prefix scoring for turn-specific remaining-return advantages with turn-mean loss aggregation, without learned critic or additional rollouts. We achieve the best aggregate scores on ProactiveVQA [25], OVO-Timing [17], and StreamingBench [15] with both Qwen backbones, and show that turn-mean aggregation improves response timing while reducing repetition relative to credit-only optimization.

sections.title: 2.1 Streaming Video Interaction
sections.content: Streaming video interaction extends offline video understanding [34] by requiring models to process incoming observations and decide when to communicate. Unlike answering after viewing an entire video, these models must operate on observed prefixes and accommodate evolving user queries. VideoLLM-online [4] introduces online video-language modeling, while MMDuet [24] broadens time-sensitive comprehension through interleaved video-text dialogue. Dispider [19] disentangles perception, decision, and reaction, and StreamBridge [23] equips offline models with lightweight proactive activation module. TimeChat-Online [28] reduces visual redundancy, while Flash-VStream [33] maintains compact memory for real-time understanding of long video streams. Streamo [27] further supports diverse streaming tasks through large-scale instruction tuning, including narration, event captioning, and time-sensitive question answering. Benchmarks including ProactiveVideoQA [25], OVO-Bench [17], and StreamingBench [15] cover real-time perception, historical understanding, and proactive response timing. These studies establish the setting for learning response and waiting decisions, while our work focuses on how RL feedback is assigned and weighted across those decisions.

sections.title: 2.2 Reinforcement Learning for Video Understanding
sections.content: PPO [20] and GRPO [21] provide widely used foundations for language-model policy optimization. Their application to video models has progressed from preference alignment to temporal reasoning and long-video training. VLM-RLAIF [1] uses AI-generated feedback for video instruction tuning. Video-R1 [9] encourages temporal reasoning through T-GRPO, VideoChat-R1 [14] strengthens spatio-temporal perception through reinforcement fine-tuning, and LongVILA-R1 [6] scales RL training to long video inputs. Policy distillation can improve initialization for subsequent RL [8, 29]. In streaming settings, MMDuet2 [26] optimizes PAUCbased interaction rewards and uses short-span training to mitigate reward sparsity and temporal credit assignment. ThinkStream [16] trains incremental reasoning with accuracy, format, and timing rewards, while StreamPro [13] combines turn-level response scores with trajectory-level coherence rewards. These approaches improve evaluation of sampled interactions, but their trajectory-level GRPO formulations derive shared advantage from the aggregated reward. TurnWise aligns streaming policy optimization with decision turns through group-relative remaining-return credit and turn-mean loss aggregation. 3 Fig. 2 Overview of TurnWise. Given streaming video input x, user queries, dialogue history, and an observation plan, the policy samples group of trajectories {τi}G i=1. TurnWise converts trajectory rewards Ri into group-relative remaining-return advantages ˆAi,t through silence-completed prefix scoring. Turn-mean aggregation then gives every response-or-wait decision equal weight in the trajectory loss Li.

sections.title: 3 Methodology
sections.content: Fig. 2 presents an overview of TurnWise. TurnWise aligns policy optimization with streaming decisions through two coupled mechanisms: group-relative remaining-return advantages and equal weighting of decision turns.

sections.title:
3.1 Streaming Decisions and Trajectory Rewards
A streaming instance comprises video input x, user queries, initial dialogue history h0, and an observation
plan specifying the decision-time grid. At decision turn t, the policy’s context hi,t contains only the available
video-text prefix and its previously generated actions in sampled trajectory i. The policy πθ generates either
a textual response or the explicit waiting output NO REPLY, denoted by ∅. Waiting produces no user-visible
answer, but remains a generated action optimized alongside responses. To learn these decisions, we sample
G trajectories τi = (ai,1, . . . , ai,Ti) from the rollout policy, with ai,t ∼ πθold (· | hi,t). Here, Ti denotes the
number of decision turns in trajectory i; aligned trajectories within a group follow the same observation plan
and have a common horizon, while different instances may have different horizons. Their observations are
shared, but their dialogue histories can differ through earlier sampled responses. Consequently, the value of
a new response depends on both the evidence available so far and the information already communicated.

(1) Here, Pi measures response quality and timeliness within annotated reply windows [25]. For given quality improvement, responding earlier increases its contribution over the window, linking answer content to response timing. The remaining terms penalize unwanted response behaviors: Drep is the fraction of non-silent replies is the fraction of out-of-window decision turns whose information is already covered by previous replies; Dout at which the model responds; and Dprefix counts excessively long shared-prefix violations normalized by Ti. Empty denominators contribute zero, and repetition checks include non-silent assistant replies in the actual initial dialogue. Broadcasting Aglobal to every action token expresses preference over whole trajectories, but does not distinguish rewards earned before turn from gains obtained from that turn onward. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Our evaluation measures benchmark performance, the complementary effects of credit assignment and loss aggregation, and the resulting changes in response behavior.

sections.title: 4.1 Training Pipeline
sections.content: We first fine-tune Qwen2.5-VL-3B [3] and Qwen3-VL-4B [2] on EgoExo4D [10], EgoExoLearn [12], LiveWhisperX [5], Tarsier2 [31], and LLaVA-Video [34]. Both models use the same SFT corpus of 100,874 valid instruction examples, with 1% held out for validation. SFT runs for one epoch at learning rate 105 with the vision tower frozen. We then optimize the streaming policies with GRPO-style reinforcement learning [21], using groups of sampled trajectories to form relative advantage signals. RL uses 3,983 streaming instances with 20-second target segments, initial dialogue context, and at most 90 frames sampled every two seconds, following MMDuet2 [26]. We use the PAUC-based reward in equation (1), judged by gpt-oss-20b [18]. All RL configurations use batch size 8 and = 4 rollouts per instance, with temperature 1.2 and top-k = 10, following MMDuet2 [26]. We train for one epoch with AdamW at learning rate 106, one policy optimization epoch per batch, and no KL or entropy regularization. TurnWise freezes the vision tower and uses turn-mean aggregation, with α linearly warmed up to 1 over the first 10% of scheduled updates. sections.title: 4.2 Benchmarks
sections.content: We evaluate on ProactiveVQA [25], using 300 instances across Ego, TV, VAD, and Web to assess answer quality and timeliness within reply windows. OVO-Timing [17] evaluates event-triggered responses on CRR, SSR, and REC. StreamingBench [15] tests answer correctness from observed video prefixes through Real-Time Visual Understanding, and joint answer correctness and timing through Proactive Output. Together, these benchmarks assess complementary aspects of streaming policies: proactive answer quality, event-triggered timing, and real-time visual understanding.

sections.title: 4.3 Evaluations
sections.content: We compare TurnWise with SFT models and the RL baselines MMDuet2, ThinkStream [16], and StreamPro [13], implemented in the same streaming GRPO framework. All models use greedy decoding with observed video prefixes and their own previous responses as context. On ProactiveVQA, we report PAUC with ω = 0.5, judged by GPT-5.6-luna and averaged equally across four categories; ablations also report repetition rates among non-silent replies. OVO-Timing uses Timing F1 with one-to-one matching within 2 seconds. We compute F1 from mean per-instance precision and recall for each task, then average equally across CRR, SSR, and REC. For StreamingBench, we report multiple-choice accuracy on Real-Time Visual Understanding and joint answer-and-timing accuracy within 2 seconds on Proactive Output, and their equal-weight mean.

sections.title: 5.2 Training Dynamics and Response Behavior
sections.content: Turn-mean aggregation raises mean reward from 0.657 to 0.711 over the final 50 updates while reducing repetition-penalty magnitude from 0.069 to 0.036 (Fig. 3, panels and b). Both configurations use the same turn-level credit rule and Qwen2.5-VL-3B SFT initialization across 497 updates. The outside-window reply fraction decreases from 0.537 to 0.289, while the non-silent decision fraction falls from 62.2% to 37.0% (panel c). Higher reward accompanies more selective response behavior under turn-mean aggregation.

decision turns. As shown in panel a of Fig. 4, 21.20% of decisions change advantage sign relative to global
allocation, and 53.15% of trajectories receive both positive and negative turn advantages. Thus, a single
trajectory provides distinct learning directions for its constituent decisions.
sections.content: This differentiation also targets redundant replies within positively ranked trajectories. Panel of Fig. 4 shows that turn-level credit increases the share receiving negative advantages from 75.7% to 81.6% across all 2,972 Judge-labeled repetitive replies in this cohort. These recorded advantages show that turn-level credit assigns distinct learning directions within trajectory and provides suppressive signals for redundant replies in positively ranked trajectories.

sections.title: 5.4 Discussion
sections.content: Tables 2 and 3 and Figs. 3 and 4 highlight complementary roles for credit assignment and loss aggregation: the former determines each turns learning signal, while the latter controls its optimization weight. Remaining10 return advantages improve credit assignment, while turn-mean aggregation balances response and waiting decisions. Their combination improves task scores and Timing F1 while reducing redundant and outsidewindow replies. TurnWise unifies credit assignment and policy optimization at the decision-turn level. deterministic scan of cached PAUC assessments computes the prefix references without additional rollouts or judge calls. Across the evaluated settings, this alignment improves task performance and response timing while reducing redundant replies.

sections.title: 6 Conclusion
sections.content: TurnWise makes the decision turn the common unit of credit assignment and policy optimization in streaming video RL. Silence-completed prefix references remove previously accrued rewards from later-turn credit, while turn-mean aggregation gives response and waiting decisions equal weight, without learned critic or additional rollouts. Across two Qwen backbones, TurnWise achieves the best aggregate results on all three evaluated benchmarks, with component analyses supporting higher-quality, better-timed, and more selective responses.
